clinicalPearls: Infection is contracted through contact with freshwater bodies harboring infected intermediate-host snails; cercariae penetrate intact human skin within a few minutes (p.1826).
A travel/migration history of freshwater exposure (bathing, washing, fishing, rice-field work, swimming) in an endemic area is central to the diagnosis, especially in travelers (p.1827, p.1829).
Most disease manifestations are due to immunologic granulomatous reactions to eggs retained in host tissues, not to the adult worms; about half of eggs are trapped in tissue (p.1827).

Cercarial dermatitis ('swimmer's itch') is a maculopapular rash from cercarial skin penetration; a severe form follows exposure to avian schistosomes (e.g., lakes in Europe/US) that die in the skin (p.1828).

Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) occurs 2 weeks to 3 months after exposure, usually in first-time-infected travelers, with fever, myalgia, malaise, headache, nonproductive cough, and abdominal symptoms (p.1828).
Eosinophilia is a common finding and is often associated with schistosomiasis; transient pulmonary infiltrates may accompany Katayama fever (p.1828, p.1829).

Intestinal schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, S. japonicum): worms in mesenteric veins; eggs trapped in intestinal tissue cause granulomatous inflammation, microulceration, intermittent abdominal pain, and sometimes bloody diarrhea (p.1829).

Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, S. japonicum): late disease produces periportal (Symmers clay-pipestem) fibrosis with portal vein occlusion, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, esophageal varices, and hematemesis; hepatic function usually remains normal (p.1827, p.1829).

Urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium): hallmark of the active stage is painless terminal hematuria, with dysuria and suprapubic discomfort; eggs in bladder mucosa cause inflammation, fibrosis, 'sandy patches', and possible ureteric obstruction with hydronephrosis (p.1829).
S. haematobium is an IARC group 1 carcinogen; chronic infection is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder (p.1829).

Detection of schistosome eggs in stool or urine indicates active infection and is the standard diagnostic method; S. haematobium eggs (terminal spine) are excreted in urine, other species (S. mansoni lateral spine, S. japonicum small lateral knob) in feces (p.1826, p.1829).

Neuroschistosomiasis is one of the most severe forms: S. mansoni/S. haematobium can cause transverse myelitis (an acute complication in returning travelers), while S. japonicum causes cerebral granulomas with seizures and focal neurologic deficits (p.1829).
harrison.pathophysiology: Free-swimming cercariae released from infected freshwater snails penetrate intact skin within minutes, transform into schistosomula, enter veins/lymphatics, traverse the lungs and heart, and mature in the portal vein into paired adult male and female worms that migrate to the mesenteric (S. mansoni, S. japonicum) or pelvic/vesical (S. haematobium) venous plexus. The prepatent period is 5-7 weeks (up to 12 for S. haematobium). About half of the eggs produced are excreted in feces or urine; the remainder become trapped in tissue. Most morbidity results from egg-induced, TH2-driven granulomatous immune responses (lymphocytes, eosinophils, alternatively activated macrophages; IL-4/5/13). Egg antigen excess early in infection forms soluble immune complexes causing a serum sickness-like illness (Katayama fever). Hepatic egg deposition leads to periportal (Symmers) fibrosis, portal-branch occlusion, and portal hypertension; S. haematobium egg deposition in the bladder/ureters causes inflammation, fibrosis, obstructive uropathy, and predisposes to squamous bladder carcinoma (p.1826-1829).
additionalDifferentials: Malaria (acute febrile illness in returning traveler/migrant) (p.1829)
Visceral larva migrans / toxocariasis (fever with eosinophilia) (p.1829)
Other causes of portal hypertension and hepatosplenomegaly, including cirrhosis (p.1829)
infectionMimics: Opisthorchis and Clonorchis (liver fluke) infections causing fever and eosinophilia (p.1829)
nonInfectiousMimics: Cirrhosis from other causes presenting with portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and variceal bleeding (p.1829)
Bladder squamous cell carcinoma from non-schistosomal causes (chronic urogenital disease) (p.1829)
additionalInvestigations: Microscopic detection of eggs in stool (e.g., ~50 mg) or urine (filtration of ~10 mL) with quantitation (eggs per gram or per 10 mL); concentration methods (e.g., formol-ether) for low-burden travelers (p.1829)
Rectal biopsy for eggs (S. mansoni and S. haematobium); occasionally Pap smears and semen samples (S. haematobium) (p.1829)
PCR-based detection of Schistosoma DNA in stool or urine (more sensitive than parasitology); CSF Schistosoma DNA for neuroschistosomiasis (p.1829)

Serology for anti-schistosome antibodies (CDC: FAST-ELISA with S. mansoni microsomal antigen plus confirmatory species-specific immunoblot) - useful in travelers, less so in endemic populations (p.1829-1830)
Circulating anodic/cathodic antigen (CAA/CCA) detection in serum or urine by ELISA or lateral flow as a marker of active infection; point-of-care urine CCA assay used in community screening (p.1830)
Ultrasonography to demonstrate periportal fibrosis, portal vein dilation, and obstructive uropathy/hydronephrosis (p.1829)
Cystoscopy showing 'sandy patches' of calcified eggs in chronic urogenital disease; endoscopy or ultrasound for esophageal varices (p.1829)
redFlags: Hematemesis or melena from esophageal varices in hepatosplenic disease - the most severe complication; death may result from massive blood loss (p.1829)
Acute transverse myelitis or other cerebral/spinal cord manifestations - neuroschistosomiasis, even from light infections (p.1829)
Severe Katayama fever with weight loss, dyspnea, diarrhea, and hepatomegaly; rarely fatal (p.1829)
Painless terminal hematuria in a traveler/migrant from an endemic area (urogenital S. haematobium) (p.1829)
Obstructive uropathy progressing to uremia from ureteral fibrosis (p.1829)
harrison.prognosis: Many patients recover spontaneously from acute schistosomiasis after 2-10 weeks, though some follow a more severe course, and the acute syndrome can rarely be fatal. In hepatosplenic disease, hepatic function usually remains normal even with marked periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension; however, severe periportal (Symmers) fibrosis is often irreversible, and hematemesis from variceal bleeding may be fatal. Early inflammatory hepatosplenomegaly in children generally decreases over time as immunity develops. Ureteral fibrosis can cause irreversible obstructive uropathy progressing to uremia. The adult worm lifespan averages 3-5 years but can reach 30 years (p.1826-1829).
pitfalls: Patients with periportal fibrosis (late hepatosplenic disease) may excrete very few or no eggs in feces, so a negative stool exam does not exclude advanced disease (p.1829).
In the chronic urogenital stage, urinary egg excretion may be sparse or absent despite ongoing urogenital tract pathology (p.1829).
Egg excretion may be very low in people from nonendemic areas (travelers), requiring larger samples and concentration methods (p.1829).
Katayama fever is rare in people chronically exposed in S. mansoni- or S. haematobium-endemic areas, so its absence does not exclude infection in residents (p.1829).
CAA/CCA antigen detection is not currently suitable for diagnosing travelers, who have low worm burdens (p.1830).
Serology is less useful in people from endemic areas with ongoing transmission (p.1829-1830).
harrison.severityClassification: Disease is staged clinically by duration and intensity of infection into three phases - acute (cercarial dermatitis and Katayama fever), active/established, and chronic (e.g., late hepatosplenic periportal fibrosis with portal hypertension, or chronic urogenital fibrosis with sandy patches and obstructive uropathy). Severity of early hepatosplenomegaly is closely associated with infection intensity (p.1828-1829).
management: Treat established infection with the antihelminthic praziquantel, which is active against the adult worms of all Schistosoma species

For acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) add corticosteroids to control the hypersensitivity reaction and repeat praziquantel once worms mature, since early treatment is less effective against immature schistosomula
In neuroschistosomiasis or spinal cord involvement give corticosteroids alongside praziquantel and arrange urgent neurological and neurosurgical assessment
Manage chronic complications by treating portal hypertension and oesophageal varices in hepatosplenic disease and relieving obstructive uropathy in urinary S. haematobium infection
Provide symptomatic antipruritic treatment for cercarial dermatitis and maintain surveillance for bladder squamous carcinoma in chronic S. haematobium infection
Advise avoidance of freshwater contact in endemic areas and support public-health measures including snail control and mass drug administration
Retest with parasitological or antigen studies after treatment and re-treat if eggs persist, screening exposed travellers and household contacts
